clue.text: * Anstey's trumpet and trombone engagement

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: F. Anstey's comic fantasy novel about a genie released from an old vessel

explanation.surface: An Anstey story is pitched as a clash between two sections of a band.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the O in BOTTLE for an A and the novel's title becomes THE BRASS BATTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Trumpets and trombones are the brass section, and an engagement in the military sense is a fight between forces.

clue.text: * Balzac's translated contribution to Tristram Shandy

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: the English title of Balzac's La Rabouilleuse, about a family's disgraced son

explanation.surface: A Balzac novel in English is pictured as a passage added to Sterne's comic novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the final P of SHEEP to T. Tristram Shandy famously prints an entirely black page to mourn Parson Yorick.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterne's novel includes a page printed solid black, so that inked leaf is literally his book's odd contribution.

clue.text: How you might be obtaining tagine

definitions.text: How you might be obtaining tagine

parts.words: How you might be obtaining tagine
parts.note: surface reading: you might get this Moroccan stew by dining at a restaurant rather than cooking
setter's reading: the dish's six letters come from a six-letter word for consuming, jumbled, with the second word acting as the shuffle signal

explanation.surface: Someone wonders how to get hold of a Moroccan stew.
explanation.walkthrough: EATING, scrambled ('out'), gives TAGINE, and EATING OUT is also how you'd order one in a restaurant.
explanation.definitionFit: Dining at a restaurant is the usual way to be served a slow-cooked North African stew without making it at home.

clue.text: * Take delight in Walter's novel

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: Sir Walter Scott's novel about a Highland outlaw

explanation.surface: A reader enjoys a novel by Walter Scott.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the second R of ROB ROY to J, giving ROB JOY.
explanation.definitionFit: To rob is to take by force and joy is delight, so the phrase reads as stealing someone's happiness.

clue.text: George and Iain feature in a book by Erskine Childers

definitions.text: feature in a book by Erskine Childers

parts.note: George Sand, the French novelist
Iain Banks, the Scottish novelist

explanation.surface: Two novelists appear as characters in a Childers spy story.
explanation.walkthrough: Childers's The Riddle of the Sands is set among the shifting shoals of the Frisian coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Shallow ridges of sediment off the German coast are central to the plot of The Riddle of the Sands.

clue.text: Brontë of a kind, a lady Jilly Copper wrote about

definitions.text: a lady Jilly Copper wrote about

parts.note: the Brontë sisters published as Currer, Ellis and Acton Bell
taken as written

explanation.surface: Jilly Cooper's heroine is likened to a Brontë.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'Copper' for Cooper, presumably a misprint; Jilly Cooper wrote the novel Bella, about an actress.
explanation.definitionFit: Bella is the title heroine of a Jilly Cooper romance, so she is literally a lady that author wrote about.

clue.text: * Zola's Waterloo?

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: Zola's novel of a miners' strike

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Zola met his own Waterloo.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the G of GERMINAL to T. Waterloo is a major London railway station.
explanation.definitionFit: Waterloo is an example of a railway station where lines end; the question mark flags a definition by example.

clue.text: Memorise Edward's bit of nonsense

parts.note: Edward Lear, the writer of nonsense verse

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone is told to learn one of Edward Lear's nonsense rhymes by heart.
explanation.definitionFit: To commit something to memory is to acquire it by study, which is what the verb means.

clue.text: Ancient giant among Kentish-men

indicators.note: something found among a group sits inside it, so the letters lie within the following words

parts.note: the three letters after the opening K

explanation.surface: A legendary giant is imagined living among the people of west Kent.
explanation.walkthrough: Kentish Men are people born west of the Medway in Kent, a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tolkien and in Old English poetry the word names a tree-like creature or a giant of the ancient world.

clue.text: * Banks gave us these boring plans

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: Iain Banks's thriller set on a ship trapped in the Panama Canal

explanation.surface: A reader grumbles that a Banks novel offered only dull schemes.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the C of CANAL to B.
explanation.definitionFit: Banal means dull and unoriginal, and dreams are aspirations or schemes for the future.

clue.text: * Salman's wicked parts on the edge

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: Salman Rushdie's controversial 1988 novel

explanation.surface: Rushdie's book is summed up as its most daring, edgy passages.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the S of VERSES to G.
explanation.definitionFit: Satanic means devilishly wicked, and verges are the borders or edges of something such as a road.

clue.text: Jargon from Christian seen in Felix Holt, mostly

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: the Rev. John Lingon, the clergyman uncle in George Eliot's Felix Holt, the Radical

explanation.surface: Jargon is attributed to a churchgoer in George Eliot's political novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Lingon, a hunting rector, is one of the novel's Christians; lose his last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal speech for the specialised vocabulary of a trade or group, which is what jargon means.

clue.text: I'm from South America and I love to read about schoolgirls

parts.note: Angela Brazil, the author whose books readers turned to for stories about schoolgirls
a nut is a fan, someone who loves a thing

explanation.surface: A South American speaker confesses a fondness for school stories.
explanation.walkthrough: Angela Brazil wrote popular early twentieth-century girls' boarding-school novels; someone who loves her books is a Brazil nut, a nut being an enthusiast.
explanation.definitionFit: The large edible seed grows wild in the Amazon rainforest, so it can say it comes from that continent.

clue.text: Poetically singing bird making a constant din

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Ted Hughes's poetry sequence centres on a black bird of the corvid family
second meaning: a cock's loud repeated call, or boastful talk

explanation.surface: A noisy bird is described as singing in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half may point to Ted Hughes's Crow; the definition as a verb is slightly loose against 'making'.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a black bird celebrated by Ted Hughes and also the verb for a cockerel's loud repeated cry.

clue.text: Against reason, sometimes

parts.note: on as in leaning on, against
an occasion is a cause or reason for something

explanation.surface: Someone sometimes acts against reason.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means now and then, from time to time, which is what 'sometimes' says.

clue.text: Corrupting 16, but not Brown

indicators.note: but not asks for the following item to be taken away from the word

parts.note: 16 is a cross-reference; its answer, ratty, has this synonym
a light brown colour

explanation.surface: A bad influence is likened to the 16 clue minus Brown.
explanation.walkthrough: 16 is IRRITABLE, whose synonym CANTANKEROUS loses TAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Cankerous describes something that eats away like an ulcer, so it is spoiling or corrupting.

clue.text: I'm ratty — I can be seen on rivers, with one on board

parts.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for river, doubled for the plural
Roman numeral one
a board is a table, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A bad-tempered speaker says they turn up on rivers with someone aboard.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening I does double duty as the speaker and the first letter; 'with one on board' puts the numeral just before the board.
explanation.definitionFit: Ratty is informal British slang for bad-tempered and easily annoyed, the same sense as the answer.

clue.text: * Golding's green baize award

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: William Golding's 1959 novel

explanation.surface: A Golding novel is reimagined as a snooker table prize.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the second F to B. In snooker, a free ball is awarded after a foul leaves the player snookered.
explanation.definitionFit: Snooker is played on green baize, and the referee awards this as a concession to the player who was fouled.

clue.text: Murdoch included, satisfying is what 19 is doing to Faust

indicators.note: included means placed within something, so the novelist goes inside

parts.note: the first part of the word for satisfying
Iris Murdoch, the novelist
the remainder of the word for satisfying

explanation.surface: An odd sentence about Murdoch and what a schoolboy does to Faust.
explanation.walkthrough: IRIS goes inside SATING. The 19 cross-reference is to ERIC; how that answer mocks Faust is not explained by the wordplay, which stands on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Mocking a work through ridicule, as a comic parody of Goethe's Faust would, means lampooning it.

clue.text: A fine schoolboy, in a gradual decline

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the earnest boarding-school hero of F. W. Farrar's Victorian novel
second meaning: the novel's full title ends 'or, Little by Little', a slow fall

explanation.surface: A good pupil slowly goes off the rails.
explanation.walkthrough: Farrar's Eric, or, Little by Little (1858) follows a decent boy's gradual moral fall.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian moral tale's hero starts as a promising pupil and declines step by step, matching both halves.

clue.text: After posterior, like a spanker?

indicators.note: the word is reduced to its opening letter, as abbreviations often are

parts.note: the first letter of the word
the stern is the rear of a ship, the posterior

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of a smacking applied to someone's bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: A spanker is the aftermost sail of a sailing ship.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's spanker is the fore-and-aft sail at the back, so it is positioned towards the rear of the vessel.

clue.text: In summer in France, a form of cornet is something savoury

indicators.note: a form of something is a new shape for it, so the letters are rearranged
in tells us one set of letters is placed inside another

parts.note: été is French for summer
the six letters rearranged

explanation.surface: An ice-cream cornet in a French summer is called savoury.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pulls towards ice cream and sweetness; été is the French for summer, and the dish is meat.
explanation.definitionFit: This French cut of steak, taken from between the ribs, is a savoury dish rather than a sweet one.

clue.text: What you may not have to receive nuts, proverbially

definitions.text: What you may not have to receive nuts, proverbially

parts.words: What you may not have to receive nuts
parts.note: surface reading: something you need not possess to be given nuts
setter's reading: the proverb says God gives nuts to those with nothing to crack them

explanation.surface: Something is not required to get nuts, according to a saying.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'God sends nuts to those who have no teeth': good fortune arrives when you can no longer enjoy it.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying names the biting tools a person lacks when given nuts, which matches the clue's description.

clue.text: Louis May's cousins, in part of a sonnet

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Louisa May Alcott wrote Eight Cousins, so her cousins are a group of eight
second meaning: the opening eight lines of a Petrarchan sonnet

explanation.surface: Family members feature in a poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue prints 'Louis' for Louisa May Alcott, whose novel is Eight Cousins.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a group of eight, so it fits the eight cousins and also the first eight lines of a sonnet.

clue.text: French composer posed next to Ireland

parts.note: sat as a model sits for a portrait
the internet country code for Ireland

explanation.surface: A French composer sat for a portrait beside an Irish one.
explanation.walkthrough: John Ireland was an English composer, which makes the surface plausible.
explanation.definitionFit: Erik Satie, who wrote the Gymnopédies, was a composer born in Normandy.

clue.text: * Ford's final attitude, in America

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: the last novel of Ford Madox Ford's Parade's End sequence

explanation.surface: Ford's closing stance is described, with a nod to America.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the final T of POST to E. 'In America' may hint that Ford's last novel was published there under that title.
explanation.definitionFit: A pose is a bodily attitude or stance, and the last one is the final position held.

clue.text: Regularly being like Weldon's women

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Something is said to resemble the women in Fay Weldon's novels.
explanation.walkthrough: Fay Weldon wrote the novel Big Women about a feminist publishing house.
explanation.definitionFit: Fay Weldon's novel is titled Big Women, so its women are described by this adjective for large.

clue.text: * Tatjana's racing car joins the contest

indicators.note: the star marks a themed clue where one letter of a book title by the named author is swapped for another

parts.note: Tatjana Soli's novel set during the Vietnam War

explanation.surface: Soli's novel is recast as a motor race with a new competitor.
explanation.walkthrough: Change the A of EATERS to N. Lotus is a British racing car maker.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lotus is a Formula One car brand, and entering a contest means joining it as a competitor.
